children: Police in Bhiwandi, Maharashtra’s Thane district, have registered an FIR against a Reliance Consumer Products director and nine others, including officials associated with Reliance Retail, Blinkit and Hyperpure, following a Food and Drug Administration (FDA) investigation into the alleged diversion of expired and rejected food products back into retail markets. The regulator seized stock worth ₹48.09 lakh during inspections across Thane and Pune districts on October 14–15 and suspended licences of five facilities linked to the companies, senior FDA officials told businessline.

The investigation centres on whether warehouse operators and disposal contractors failed to ensure that expired, damaged and customer-rejected food products were destroyed. Instead, the goods were allegedly diverted through unlicensed sorting yards, brokers and retailers before reaching consumers, the officials said.

The FIR, registered at Shanti Nagar police station, names V. Subramaniam, whole-time director of Reliance Consumer Products, alongside officials associated with Reliance Retail, Blinkit and Eternal’s business-to-business food-supplies arm Hyperpure. Others named include a disposal-agency operator, local suppliers and a discount-store owner. The case invokes provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act and Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.

Seven FDA teams conducted coordinated inspections across Thane and Pune districts. Following hearings on October 15, the regulator suspended licences of Reliance Consumer Products and Reliance Retail facilities at Vadpe in Bhiwandi, a Reliance Retail warehouse at Chakan, Hyperpure’s Usatane facility and a Blinkit warehouse at Nighoje. The suspensions are facility-specific rather than company-wide.

The largest reported seizure, worth over ₹24 lakh, came from a Bhiwandi disposal yard. Officials also seized approximately ₹4.92 lakh of stock at Reliance Consumer Products’ Vadpe warehouse and ₹7.81 lakh at Hyperpure’s Usatane facility.

According to FDA officials, disposal agencies allegedly issued destruction certificates without adequately verifying that rejected goods had actually been destroyed. At unlicensed sorting yards, packets appearing saleable were separated and supplied to brokers and retailers. Expired and leaking products were subsequently found displayed for sale at an unlicensed Bhiwandi outlet.
Investigators also found alleged quantity mismatches and inconsistent consignor-consignee details in disposal records, raising questions about oversight of third-party contractors.

The case follows earlier FDA action against Amazon Retail India’s Bhiwandi warehouse over similar allegations. Its licence was suspended in June and subsequently cancelled. Amazon challenged the action in the Bombay High Court, which questioned the regulator’s approach and later ordered an interim arrangement for scientific disposal of expired stock.

Investigators must now establish whether warehouse operators verified actual destruction of rejected stock and determine responsibility across the disposal chain. The allegations remain under investigation.

title: Reliance Consumer Director, Blinkit officials among 10 booked in expired-food probe
